summary: This standards-track document specifies XML syntax and processing for Evidence Records, which show existence and integrity of data over long periods. It supports long-term non-repudiation, including signed data.

eli5.summary: A time stamp book that proves a document existed and hasn't changed, readable for decades, written in XML.

questions: how does hash tree renewal work
how to prove data existed long term
subtitle: An XML format and set of rules for keeping time-stamped proof that data existed and has not changed, for decades.

tldr.problem: Digital signatures and time-stamps weaken over time as algorithms get broken, certificates expire and services close, yet some data must be provable as existing and unchanged for long or undetermined periods.
tldr.mechanism: An Evidence Record collects Archive Time-Stamps, each a time-stamp token plus an optional hash tree, and renews them before they expire. A new time-stamp covers either the last time-stamp or, when the hash algorithm changes, the data and the whole earlier sequence.
tldr.outcome: XMLERS gives the same kind of long-term proof as the ASN.1 Evidence Record Syntax of RFC 4998, in XML. It is a Proposed Standard and is not marked as obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 6283 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the XML counterpart to the ASN.1 syntax of RFC 4998.

sections.title: Why Long-Term Evidence Is Needed
sections.content:
Electronic commerce needs non-repudiable proof that data existed and kept its integrity, and that proof must last, even when the original proof weakens or ceases to exist. Digital signatures such as those in RFC 5652 do not give absolute reliability over the long term. Algorithms can become weak, and the information needed to validate a signature can be compromised or vanish, for example when a certificate service provider disbands. Time-stamping suffers from the same decay, including a Time-Stamping Authority going out of business.

The Extensible Markup Language Evidence Record Syntax (XMLERS) addresses this by giving the same approach as the ASN.1 Evidence Record Syntax in RFC 4998, but in XML. It is not a direct transformation: it has its own processing rules, does not support importing ASN.1 values into XML tags, and is a standalone document that is based on RFC 4998 only conceptually. It follows the long-term archive requirements in RFC 4810.

Long-term signature formats protect the signatures themselves. Evidence Records extend this to data of any type or format, including digital signatures. An Evidence Record can be embedded in the data or stored separately as a standalone XML file.
sections.eli5: Signatures and stamps get old and can stop being trustworthy. This RFC describes a way to keep adding fresh proof, written in XML, so the proof outlasts the things it was built from.

sections.title: Key Concepts
sections.content:
An archive data object is a unit of data to preserve, and an archive object (AO) is either one data object or a group of them. A Long-Term Archive (LTA) is the service that generates, collects and renews the evidence. It gets time-stamp tokens from a Time-Stamping Authority (TSA), for example in the form defined by RFC 3161.

An Archive Time-Stamp (ATS) is a time-stamp token plus data useful for validating it, and optionally a hash tree: ordered lists of hash values. A series of successive ATSs forms an Archive Time-Stamp Chain (ATSC), and a series of chains forms an Archive Time-Stamp Sequence (ATSSeq). An Evidence Record is the whole collection of evidence kept for an archive object over time.

Time-stamps under RFC 3161 cover a single unit of data and have no rules for keeping a time-stamp stable over the long term. XMLERS adds those rules. It uses a hash tree, a technique credited to Merkle, so that one time-stamp can protect many archive objects. Only the root hash is time-stamped, deleting one data object does not affect the provability of the others, and the tree can be reduced to the few hash values needed to prove one object.
sections.eli5: Think of a stack of documents, a notary stamp, and a fresh stamp laid over the old one every so often. The names in this RFC are just labels for the pieces: the thing kept, the stamp, a row of stamps, and the whole scrapbook.

sections.title: The Evidence Record Structure
sections.content:
The root element is <EvidenceRecord>, with a required Version attribute (the current version is 1.0). It may contain an optional <EncryptionInformation>, an optional <SupportingInformationList> and a required <ArchiveTimeStampSequence>. The schema uses the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:ers.

Each <ArchiveTimeStampChain> has a required <DigestMethod>, a required <CanonicalizationMethod> and one or more <ArchiveTimeStamp> elements. Each ATS holds an optional <HashTree>, a required <TimeStamp> (with a <TimeStampToken> and an optional <CryptographicInformationList>) and optional <Attributes>.

Because XML gives no unambiguous way to order same-named sibling elements, an Order attribute is REQUIRED whenever several elements of the same name sit at one level, and chains and time-stamps MUST be ordered by it. Digest values depend on that order.

Anything that is already known at the time of a renewal, such as a cryptographic policy, SHOULD go into the individual ATS's <Attributes>, because later time-stamps protect it. Information relevant to the whole record, or that arrived later, can go in <SupportingInformationList>, which is not protected by any time-stamp.
sections.eli5: It is a binder. The front has a label for the version, then pages for each stamp, with a note for which stamp came first, second and third, because the order matters.

sections.title: Hash Trees and the First Time-Stamp
sections.content:
A <HashTree> is a list of <Sequence> elements, each with base64-encoded <DigestValue> elements. To compute the root, decode the values of the first sequence, sort them in binary ascending order, concatenate them and hash the result. That hash joins the next sequence's list and the step repeats until one value remains, which MUST equal the time-stamped value. If the first sequence has only one value, that value is simply added to the next list.

To build the initial ATS, the LTA collects the archive objects, picks a canonicalization method and a digest algorithm (the same one used in the time-stamp token and the hash tree), builds the tree and gets a time-stamp for the root hash. The tree can be left out when an archive object is a single data object, in which case the time-stamped value MUST match that object's digest. A group of data objects is represented by the digest of its sorted, concatenated member digests, and the first list of its tree MUST contain exactly those member hashes.

For many archive objects under one time-stamp, a full tree is built from the leaves up, and then reduced for each object: keep the object's hash, then for each level the sibling hashes under the same parent, one new <Sequence> per level with Order increased by one, until the root. Node values are not stored because they can be computed. Equal numbers of children per node are RECOMMENDED for processing, and the tree MAY be padded with arbitrary values for that.

Verification of an initial ATS hashes each data object, checks the hashes appear in the first sequence, recomputes the root, compares it with the time-stamped value and checks the time-stamp token. Any failure ends in a negative result.
sections.eli5: Imagine pairing up fingerprints of many documents, then fingerprinting each pair, again and again until one final fingerprint remains. Only that last one gets stamped. To prove one document, you just show the few fingerprints along its path to the top.

sections.title: Renewal, Chains and Verification
sections.content:
Before the latest time-stamp's algorithms weaken or its certificates are invalidated, the LTA MUST renew. There are two ways, depending on the reason. In time-stamp renewal, used when the digest algorithm stays the same, the complete last <TimeStamp> element (plus any added cryptographic information needed for its long-term validation) is canonicalized, hashed and time-stamped. The new ATS goes at the end of the current chain with its order increased by one.

In hash tree renewal, used when the digest algorithm changes, a new hash covers the hashes of all data objects, computed with the new algorithm, together with the hash of the whole canonicalized <ArchiveTimeStampSequence>. The new ATS starts a new chain, with order 1, appended to the sequence. A new chain MUST also be started when the TSA changes algorithms, using an equal or stronger digest algorithm. Within one chain the digest algorithm MUST be the same.

The algorithm is named by a URI in <DigestMethod>, and canonical XML is the way to get a binary form of XML for hashing. Canonicalization MUST be applied to XML archive data and to the ATS and ATSC elements in renewal. The RFC recommends the Canonical XML 1.0 algorithm identified by c14n-20010315.

To verify a whole record, the verifier checks the initial ATS, checks every ATS in every chain (each must have been valid at the time of the next one, and each first hash list must contain the hash of the previous time-stamp or sequence), and finally that the last ATS is valid at verification time. Only that last one needs to be monitored for expiry.
sections.eli5: When the old stamp is about to fade, you put a fresh stamp on top of it. If even the kind of ink has to change, you start a new page and stamp the old pages and the document together again.

sections.title: Encryption and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Evidence Records protect the exact bit stream. If clients send only encrypted data to an archive, the record refers to the encrypted objects, and a different key or algorithm might decrypt to something else, so the record would not prove the plain data. Only encryption methods that tie the encrypted data unambiguously to the original SHOULD be used, and the optional <EncryptionInformation> element stores the parameters so the data can be re-encrypted for validation. How it is used depends on other specifications.

Security considerations say that algorithms must be secure at the time each time-stamp is generated, and that weakening algorithms could end a record's validity with no retroactive fix. Since many TSAs use the same algorithms, a weakness hits many at once. The RFC therefore RECOMMENDS at least two redundant Evidence Records for a data object, with SHOULD-different hash algorithms and different TSAs using different cryptographic algorithms.

Renewed time-stamps MUST be of the same or higher quality as the initial one. At renewal it MUST be ascertained that the earlier time-stamp's certificate was not revoked for key compromise; other revocation reasons such as ceasing operation are not necessarily a risk. After a renewal, earlier ATS structures are frozen and nothing may be added to them.
sections.eli5: Use more than one witness and different kinds of ink, so if one kind fails, you still have another record. And always make sure the old witness was honest before you add a new stamp on top.

sections.title: Registries and Versioning
sections.content:
The RFC registers the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:ers and the XML schema urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:ers, and creates an IANA registry named "XML Evidence Record Syntax (XMLERS)" with two sub-registries. "Time-Stamp Token Type" starts with RFC3161 and XMLENTRUST. "Cryptographic Information Type" starts with CERT, CRL, OCSP and SCVP. Future assignments to both use the "RFC Required" policy.

Versions are written <major>.<minor>, compared as separate integers, so 2.4 is lower than 2.13. The major number goes up only when an older implementation could not cope by ignoring unknown elements. The minor number goes up when significant new capabilities, such as new optional elements, are added.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of the kinds of stamps and proofs allowed, and version numbers work like page counters where 2.13 comes after 2.4.
